title: A $5,000 Goku
summary: A performance by mass-produced humanoids during China’s Lunar New Year marks a turning point: robots are becoming cultural actors, and the public is growing more comfortable with them.
content:
On Lunar New Year’s Day in 2026, the CCTV Spring Festival Gala began. Across all media, it draws more than ten billion views every year. People saw Goku. Goku swinging a sword atop his Flying Nimbus. But this Goku was not an actor. It was an H2 humanoid robot from Unitree Robotics. The Flying Nimbus was a moving platform supported by four-legged robot dogs. What makes this scene matter is not the robots’ technical sophistication. It is that a machine gave flesh to a being humans imagined thousands of years ago and took the stage. Machines have begun dreaming human dreams on our behalf.

Performance has always been seen as an exclusively human domain. Art rested on the premise that acting comes from emotion, and emotion comes from consciousness. Robots assembling parts or welding cars did not unsettle us. But when robots pick up swords, perform comedy, and dance in formation, a different kind of discomfort arrives. That discomfort is not fear. It is the collapse of categories. The sense that the list of things we believed “only humans can do” is being erased, one item at a time. The sound of cracks in the hierarchy of existence.

The technical abilities of the robots in this year’s gala make the pace of change tangible. MagicLab’s MagicBot Z1 performed a Thomas 360, a move even gymnasts find difficult. Unitree’s H1 did an aerial flip at a height of three meters and completed seven and a half airflare rotations. Noetix’s robots landed backflips and sideflips precisely on a cramped comedy stage. But these robots did not create their movements from nothing. They learned from the movement data of thousands of martial artists, gymnasts, and dancers. So whose movements were those, really, when Goku swung his sword atop the Flying Nimbus?

The price is even more surprising. Unitree, whose robot played Goku on the Spring Festival stage, is already selling a humanoid robot called the R1 for between $4,900 and $5,900. The price of a single high-end home appliance. Tesla has set a target price of $20,000 for Optimus. In 2025 alone, more than 22,000 humanoid robots shipped worldwide, and over 80 percent were made in China. These are not prototypes in a lab. They are products rolling out of factories. The performance onstage was remarkable because it was not a demo of some distant future, but a showcase for an industry already in mass production.

It matters that China chose this setting. The Spring Festival Gala is the most-watched single broadcast in the world. It is not a technology fair or a conference for experts. It is a holiday show that whole families sit down to watch together. And that is where they put the robots. This is not a display of technology. It is a cultural vaccination. Injecting the antigen of robots into the antibody of the warmest, most widely shared holiday, so that society as a whole accepts them without resistance. Distributing technology not as ideology, but as memories. More powerful than laws, policies, or norms.

When a bionic robot replica of comedian Cai Ming appeared, the audience reportedly laughed. It is a strange scene when you think about it. A robot made in the exact likeness of a real person stands onstage, and people laugh. Laughter is the safest scream we let out when boundaries collapse. Rather than naming our discomfort, we laugh it off and blur the boundary. We are already growing accustomed to that boundary. Integration begins where awkwardness disappears.

Looking back at the history of technology, its deepest inroads have always come through entertainment. Radio, television, and the internet were all introduced as tools for productivity, but they changed our lives when they took the form of entertainment. Yet all of them were tools used by humans. This time is different. The robot stood onstage not as a tool, but as an actor. It is not that a piano replaced a pianist. It is as if the piano stood up on its own and began playing Chopin. We have crossed a threshold fundamentally different from past technological changes.

What if, at the Spring Festival Gala in 2040, the robot actors are no longer performing human stories? What if they perform their own emotions, their own narratives? The human audience does not understand those emotions, and the robots do not try to make themselves understood for the humans’ sake. Would that still be art? Or would that be the moment when, having handed over the stage, we find ourselves sitting in the audience? Art forms have always been redefined by technology. The question is not whether art survives, but whom that art is for.

It becomes clearer when we list what has already happened. In 2023, robots walked up and down stairs. In 2024, they began to run. In 2025, they handled tools, and more than 20,000 shipped from factories in a single year. In early 2026, they played Goku on the Spring Festival stage. We live in an age when a $5,000 robot performs a myth thousands of years old. At this pace of acceleration, predicting 2030 is not difficult. That very ease is the point. Just a few years ago, we would have classified these predictions as science fiction. Now we are not imagining the future. We are simply reading the next box on a roadmap already laid out.

Ten billion gazes watched that scene with laughter, wonder, and applause. To some, it was a triumph of technology. To others, holiday entertainment. To still others, the beginning of unease. But whatever the reaction, one thing happened across the board. The place robots occupy in people’s minds changed. Technology’s ultimate victory comes not amid cheers, but amid indifference. When the day comes that no one finds it remarkable anymore, the change is already complete. The 2026 Spring Festival Gala was the night that countdown began.

To all rabbit hole subscribers, Happy New Year!
